items.item: A buffer is pinned while in use and unpinned when a backend is done with it; a pinned buffer can never be chosen as a victim, which is the whole reason pin/unpin bookkeeping exists before any replacement policy runs at all.

at.step: Reveal: the buffer pool's own clock sweep, read directly off a real cluster

items.item: Clock-sweep with a usage counter is a cheap approximation of LRU: it avoids a system-wide lock on every access by only requiring the per-buffer spinlock already needed to pin, trading perfect recency ordering for a counter that caps out at a small fixed value.

at.step: Reveal: repeated access raises a real buffer's usage count to its own cap

items.item: A plain sequential scan is the textbook case where LRU-style policies fail badly: every page is touched exactly once, so ranking by recency alone would evict the whole working set of every other query just to make room for pages that will never be revisited.

at.step: Predict: does a sequential scan bigger than the whole buffer pool evict most of it?

items.item: A buffer ring isn't a separate allocation outside the normal buffer pool; it's a small, reused subset of the very same shared buffers, chosen by the normal clock-sweep algorithm and then deliberately kept small so the scan can't grow past it.

at.step: Reveal: a real, bigger-than-the-pool table's measured footprint, ring-bounded

items.item: Dirty-page tracking exists so a checkpoint (or the background writer) knows which buffers actually need a write; a buffer that was only ever read, never modified, costs nothing to evict.

at.step: Reveal: a dirtied buffer, read directly, cleaned by a real checkpoint

items.item: Double caching costs real memory (the same bytes held twice, once by the kernel and once by the engine) but buys crash safety for free, since the OS page cache survives a backend crash that would otherwise lose anything cached only in a process's own memory.

at.step: Reveal: double caching, and the flag that bypasses it

items.item: O_DIRECT isn't free: an engine that bypasses the OS cache has to do its own readahead, its own write-back scheduling and its own alignment handling, work the kernel was doing for it.

at.step: Reveal: double caching, and the flag that bypasses it

items.item: An asynchronous I/O subsystem (io_method) attacks a different problem than the buffer-ring strategy: the ring bounds how much memory a big scan uses, while async I/O lets the engine queue several reads at once instead of blocking on one read(2) call at a time.

at.step: Reveal: a genuinely newer cluster's own async I/O, measured for real

items.item: pg_buffercache and pg_stat_io read fundamentally different things: pg_buffercache reads live shared-buffer headers directly (no flush needed), while pg_stat_io is a cumulative, periodically-flushed statistics view — conflating the two leads to false negatives when checking a backend's own just-run query.

A dirty page sitting in the buffer pool is lost the instant the process crashes unless something records the write durably first — the buffer pool alone guarantees nothing about durability, only about avoiding unnecessary disk reads.

This topic is the cache layer every later Chapter 5 topic assumes exists underneath it: WAL durability, checkpoints, B-tree page access and MVCC version visibility all read and write through the exact same pinned, clock-swept buffer pool this topic opens.
